concept.overview: Git is a distributed version control system (DVCS) that records snapshots of your project over time, letting many people work on the same codebase in parallel without overwriting each other. Every clone is a full repository with complete history, so work continues offline and no single server is a point of failure. GitHub is a cloud platform built on top of Git that adds collaboration features: remote hosting, pull requests, code review, issues, and automation via GitHub Actions.
concept.whyItMatters: Version control is the backbone of every DevOps workflow. It is the single source of truth for application code, infrastructure-as-code, pipeline definitions, and documentation. Reliable branching, review, and rollback are what make continuous integration and continuous delivery safe. Without Git there is no reproducible history, no auditable change trail, and no automated pipeline trigger.
useCases: Tracking every change to application and infrastructure code with full history and blame
Enabling parallel feature development through branches and merging
Code review and quality gates via pull requests before code reaches main
Triggering CI/CD pipelines automatically on push or merge
Rolling back to a known-good commit when a release goes wrong
concept.architecture: Picture three areas on your machine and one in the cloud. (1) Working Directory: the actual files you edit. (2) Staging Area / Index: a snapshot you have marked with 'git add' as ready to commit. (3) Local Repository (.git): the committed history stored as a directed acyclic graph of commits, each pointing to its parent. Arrows flow: edit -> git add -> git commit. (4) Remote Repository (GitHub): a shared copy you sync with via 'git push' (send commits up) and 'git fetch'/'git pull' (bring commits down). Branches are lightweight movable pointers to commits; HEAD points to your current branch.

definitions.def: A project tracked by Git, including all files and the complete history in the .git directory.
An immutable snapshot of the staged changes, identified by a SHA hash and linked to its parent commit(s).
A movable pointer to a commit; used to develop features in isolation from the main line.
A reference to the commit (usually via the current branch) that your working directory is based on.
A named reference to another copy of the repository, such as 'origin' on GitHub.
Merge joins two branches creating a merge commit; rebase replays your commits on top of another branch for a linear history.
A GitHub feature to propose, review, and discuss changes on a branch before merging into the target branch.

commands.desc: Create a new local repository in the current directory.
Copy a remote repository, including its full history, to your machine.
Show which files are staged, unstaged, or untracked.
Stage changes for the next commit; use '.' for everything.
Record staged changes as a new commit with a message.
Create a new branch; 'git switch -c <name>' creates and switches.
Integrate another branch into the current one.
Replay current branch commits on top of another branch.
Send local commits to the remote and set upstream tracking.
Fetch and merge changes from the tracked remote branch.
Create a new commit that undoes a previous commit safely.

bestPractices: Write small, focused commits with clear, imperative messages ('Add retry logic', not 'fixed stuff').
Never commit directly to main on a team; use short-lived feature branches and pull requests.
Pull/rebase frequently to keep your branch close to main and reduce merge conflicts.
Add a .gitignore early so build artifacts, secrets, and node_modules never get committed.
Protect the main branch with required reviews and passing CI checks.
pitfalls: Committing secrets (API keys, .env files) — history is permanent and hard to scrub.
Force-pushing to a shared branch and overwriting teammates' commits.
Giant commits that mix unrelated changes, making review and revert painful.
Confusing 'git reset --hard' (destroys work) with 'git revert' (safe undo).
Ignoring merge conflict markers and committing them into the code.
cheatSheet: Undo last commit but keep changes: git reset --soft HEAD~1
Discard local changes to a file: git checkout -- <file>
Stash work in progress: git stash / restore with git stash pop
See who changed a line: git blame <file>
Amend the last commit message: git commit --amend
Create a lightweight tag: git tag v1.0.0 && git push origin v1.0.0

quiz.question: Which command stages a modified file for the next commit?
quiz.explanation: 'git add' moves changes into the staging area (index); 'git commit' then records them.

quiz.question: Every Git clone contains the full project history, not just the latest snapshot.
quiz.explanation: Git is distributed: each clone is a complete repository with the entire commit history.

quiz.question: What does 'git revert <sha>' do?
options: Creates a new commit that undoes the referenced commit
Resets the branch pointer without changing files
quiz.explanation: git revert is the safe way to undo: it adds a new inverse commit, preserving history.

quiz.question: Which statement about merge vs rebase is correct?
options: Rebase produces a linear history by replaying commits
quiz.explanation: Rebase replays commits onto a new base for a linear history; merge creates a merge commit.

quiz.question: Force-pushing to a shared branch can overwrite teammates' commits.
quiz.explanation: A force push can rewrite remote history and discard others' work, so avoid it on shared branches.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of a .gitignore file?
options: List files Git should not track
quiz.explanation: .gitignore tells Git which paths to leave untracked (build output, secrets, dependencies).

quiz.question: You committed an API key by mistake and already pushed. What is the BEST first response?
options: Do nothing; it's already public so it's fine
Rotate/revoke the key immediately, then remove it from history
Just delete the file in a new commit
Force-push over the branch and hope no one noticed
quiz.explanation: The key must be treated as compromised: revoke it first, then scrub history (e.g., git filter-repo). Deleting in a new commit leaves it in history.

quiz.question: Which command shows a compact visual history?
quiz.explanation: git log --oneline --graph renders a condensed, branch-aware commit graph.

quiz.question: In 'git push -u origin feature', what does '-u' do?
quiz.explanation: -u (--set-upstream) links the local branch to origin/feature so future 'git push'/'git pull' need no arguments.

quiz.question: A pull request has failing CI checks but an approving review. Your branch protection requires passing checks. What happens?
options: It can be merged because it was approved
It cannot be merged until checks pass
The checks are ignored on approval
quiz.explanation: Branch protection with required status checks blocks merge until CI passes, regardless of approvals.

quiz.question: 'git reset --hard' can permanently discard uncommitted work.
quiz.explanation: --hard resets the working directory and index to the target commit, discarding local changes.

quiz.question: What is HEAD in Git?
options: The first commit in a repo
A reference to the current commit/branch you are on
The name of the default branch
quiz.explanation: HEAD points to your current position in history, usually via the checked-out branch.

quiz.question: Two developers edited the same lines and a merge reports a conflict. What must you do?
options: Run git push --force to resolve it
Manually edit the conflicted files, remove markers, then add and commit
Delete the branch and start over
Ignore it; Git resolves conflicts automatically
quiz.explanation: Git cannot auto-resolve overlapping edits; you edit the file, remove conflict markers, stage, and commit.

tasks.title: Create your first repository
tasks.goal: Initialize a repo, make commits, and view history.
steps: Run 'git init' in a new folder
Create a README.md and add some text
Stage it with 'git add README.md'
Commit with a clear message
Run 'git log --oneline' to see your commit
successCriteria: git log shows at least one commit
git status reports a clean working tree

tasks.title: Branch, commit, and merge
tasks.goal: Practice isolated feature development and merging.
steps: Create a branch 'feature/greeting' and switch to it
Add a new file and commit it
Switch back to main
Merge the feature branch into main
Delete the feature branch
successCriteria: git log --graph shows the merge or fast-forward

tasks.title: Resolve a merge conflict
tasks.goal: Deliberately create and resolve a conflict.
steps: On main, edit line 1 of a file and commit
Create a branch from the previous commit and edit the same line differently, commit
Merge the branch into main to trigger a conflict
Open the file, choose the correct resolution, remove conflict markers
Stage and commit the resolution
successCriteria: No conflict markers remain in the file
git status shows the merge is complete

tasks.title: Open a pull request with review gates
tasks.goal: Simulate a real team workflow on GitHub.
steps: Push a feature branch to GitHub
Open a pull request targeting main
Enable branch protection requiring one review and passing checks
Add a CI workflow that runs a lint or test step
Merge only after the check passes and the PR is approved
successCriteria: PR merged into main via the GitHub UI
Merge was blocked until the required check passed
